contextTopics.label: Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine
background: Russland überfiel die Ukraine am 24. Februar 2022 in vollem Umfang. Vorausgegangen war die Annexion der Krim im März 2014 und der von Russland unterstützte bewaffnete Konflikt im Donbas ab April 2014.

Die UN-Generalversammlung verurteilte den Angriff am 2. März 2022 mit 141 zu 5 Stimmen und forderte den sofortigen Rückzug. Die EU, die USA und weitere Staaten verhängten seither mehrere Sanktionspakete.
Der Internationale Strafgerichtshof erließ im März 2023 einen Haftbefehl gegen Wladimir Putin wegen der Verschleppung ukrainischer Kinder.
Österreich ist militärisch neutral, beteiligt sich aber an den EU-Sanktionen und leistet humanitäre Hilfe. Waffenlieferungen erfolgen nicht.

contextTopics.label: Krieg in Gaza und im Nahen Osten
background: Die Hamas verübte am 7. Oktober 2023 einen Großangriff auf Israel mit rund 1.200 Toten und etwa 250 Verschleppten. Israel begann daraufhin eine großangelegte Militäroperation im Gazastreifen.
Der Konflikt reicht weit zurück: Israel wurde 1948 gegründet, es folgten mehrere Kriege mit arabischen Nachbarstaaten. Der Gazastreifen wird seit 2007 von der Hamas kontrolliert.
Der Internationale Gerichtshof befasst sich seit Dezember 2023 mit einer Klage Südafrikas wegen mutmaßlichen Völkermords; ein Urteil in der Hauptsache steht aus.

Zahlenangaben zu Opfern stammen je nach Meldung von unterschiedlichen Stellen — der von der Hamas geführten Gesundheitsbehörde, israelischen Angaben oder UN-Organisationen. Sie sind selten unabhängig überprüfbar.

contextTopics.label: Handelskonflikte und Zölle
background: Die USA erhoben ab 2018 unter Präsident Trump Zölle auf Stahl, Aluminium und zahlreiche chinesische Waren. China antwortete mit Gegenzöllen. Teile davon blieben auch unter der Nachfolgeregierung bestehen.
Die EU ist als Zollunion für die Handelspolitik ihrer Mitgliedsstaaten zuständig — Österreich verhandelt also nicht selbst, sondern die Europäische Kommission.
Zölle wirken auf zwei Wegen: Sie verteuern eingeführte Waren für Verbraucher im Einfuhrland und treffen Exporteure im Ausland. Wer die Kosten trägt, ist wirtschaftswissenschaftlich umstritten.

contextTopics.label: Inflation und Zinspolitik der EZB
background: Die Europäische Zentralbank hat als vorrangiges Ziel Preisstabilität, definiert als 2 Prozent Inflation mittelfristig. Sie steuert darüber den Leitzins für den gesamten Euroraum.
Nach Jahren mit Null- und Negativzinsen begann die EZB im Juli 2022 mit Zinserhöhungen, um die stark gestiegene Inflation zu dämpfen — ausgelöst unter anderem durch Energiepreise und Lieferengpässe.

Österreich lag bei der Inflationsrate über Jahre über dem Euroraum-Durchschnitt. Die Gründe dafür sind umstritten; genannt werden unter anderem Energiepreise, Mietanpassungen und der Gastronomiesektor.

contextTopics.label: Klimapolitik und Klimaziele
background: Im Pariser Abkommen von 2015 verpflichteten sich fast alle Staaten, die Erderwärmung deutlich unter 2 Grad gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau zu halten und 1,5 Grad anzustreben.
Die EU hat sich auf Klimaneutralität bis 2050 festgelegt und Zwischenziele für 2030 beschlossen. Österreich strebt Klimaneutralität bis 2040 an — früher als die EU-Vorgabe.

Der Weltklimarat IPCC fasst regelmäßig den Forschungsstand zusammen. Dass die Erwärmung überwiegend menschengemacht ist, gilt dort als gesichert; umstritten sind Tempo, regionale Folgen und Gegenmaßnahmen.

contextTopics.label: Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz
background: Die Europäische Kommission legte 2021 den Entwurf für den AI Act vor, die weltweit erste umfassende Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz. Er stuft Anwendungen nach Risiko ein und verbietet einige ganz.
Das Gesetz gilt für Anbieter, die ihre Systeme im EU-Markt anbieten — unabhängig davon, wo sie sitzen. Die Pflichten greifen gestaffelt über mehrere Jahre.
Kritik kommt von zwei Seiten: Teilen der Industrie, die Wettbewerbsnachteile befürchten, und Bürgerrechtsorganisationen, denen die Ausnahmen für Sicherheitsbehörden zu weit gehen.

contextTopics.label: Österreichische Innenpolitik
background: Österreich ist eine parlamentarische Demokratie. Der Nationalrat mit 183 Abgeordneten wird alle fünf Jahre gewählt; die Regierung braucht dessen Vertrauen.
Der Bundespräsident wird direkt gewählt, ernennt die Regierung und kann sie entlassen — eine Befugnis, die historisch selten genutzt wurde.
Untersuchungsausschüsse sind ein Minderheitsrecht: Ein Viertel der Abgeordneten kann einen einsetzen, ohne Zustimmung der Mehrheit.

contextTopics.label: Raiffeisen Bank International
background: Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) ist eine der größten Banken Österreichs mit Schwerpunkt in Zentral- und Osteuropa. Sie ging 2010 aus der Fusion von RZB-Teilen und Raiffeisen International hervor.
Der Raiffeisen-Sektor ist genossenschaftlich aufgebaut: lokale Raiffeisenbanken, darüber Landesbanken, darüber die RBI. Diese Struktur erklärt, warum Entscheidungen oft mehrere Ebenen betreffen.
Das Russland-Geschäft der RBI steht seit dem Angriff auf die Ukraine unter besonderer Beobachtung von EZB und US-Behörden. Ein Rückzug wurde mehrfach angekündigt und verzögerte sich.

items.title: Released isn't Realized
items.summary: Most teams have a pretty good view on their next release date. Almost no team has a date to check whether users got the benefit. From the Scrum Guide: "Each element of the framework serves a specific purpose that is essential to the overall value and results realized with Scrum." The Cambridge Dictionary defines realize as "to achieve things you hope for or plan for." Hold that against how teams usually count. They plan an item, build it, release it and call it done. A release puts something in the hands of users, and that's where realizing value and results can start. Value is realized when the users get the outcome and the benefit you expected, and your team has the evidence to show it. So in my classes and in coaching, I ask: how do you know the value of what you released was realized? It usually goes silent. The honest answer people give me is that it just isn't monitored. The team keeps producing, and nobody knows whether what it made gets used, let alone whether users get the benefit it was meant to bring. And what you expect often doesn't happen. When Microsoft tested ideas in controlled experiments, less than a third moved the metric they were designed to improve (Kohavi and colleagues, 2013). The rest made no difference or made things worse. A team that never checks can't tell which of its releases landed. It plans the next ones on guesses. Teams that do check get something back. DORA's 2023 Accelerate State of DevOps report found that teams with a strong user focus have 40% higher organizational performance. That focus includes using user feedback to decide what comes next, and judging a team's success by the value it brings users. It's survey data, so treat it as direction, and let your own releases show whether it holds for you. The evidence you collect after a release also guides you in what to build next. Try this with your team: Pick one item you released in the last few months. What benefit did you expect users to get? Was it achieved? What evidence do you have? If the answer is "we don't know", agree on one way to find out, and plan it into the next Sprint. Then take one upcoming item. Before you start, write down the benefit you expect and how you'll know it was achieved. Make setting up the monitoring and alerting for it part of building the item, and add "check the benefit" to the Product Backlog for after the release. I hope you find value in these short articles and if you are looking for more clarifications, feel free to make contact. Don't want to miss any of these blog posts? Have the “The Scrum Guide Explored” series weekly in your mailbox . Wishing you an inspiring read and a wonderful journey. Scrum on! Image

items.title: Planning Poker
items.summary: Image One of the practical activities that Scrum Teams do is Estimation, which helps the team pick an appropriate amount of work for the Sprint based on their real capacity. One of the widely used estimation techniques is Planning Poker. Let’s see how to play Planning Poker. Planning Poker When we estimate, we need to use some units for estimation. Here, units like Story Points, T-shirt Size, and Fruit Size come to life. So, you use Planning Poker to do estimation, and results will be based on one of those relative units. First of all, you need a deck of cards. The most famous deck of cards has numbers based on the modified Fibonacci sequence. Fibonacci sequence says each element is the sum of the two previous elements, and as it gets bigger, the difference with the previous element gets bigger. Like 1+2=3 2+3=5 But when you go to the higher numbers, you don’t see the exact rule. For example 8+13=21 But the next element in Planning Poker is 20. Because of that, it is said it is based on the modified Fibonacci sequence. According to the estimation unit, you will have various decks of cards. Let’s get started with cards for Story Points but first what a Story Point itself is. What is Story Point? Story Points are estimates of the relative overall effort required to fully implement a PBI influenced by the following factors: • The amount of work to do • The complexity of the work • Any risk or uncertainty in doing the work When we estimate with Story Points, we assign a point value to each item. The absolute values we assign are unimportant. You can use a modified Fibonacci sequence (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, …) or a doubling sequence (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …). What matters are the relative values. A PBI with 2 Story Points should be twice as much effort as a 1 Story Point. It should be one-fourth of a PBI that is estimated as 8 Story Points. Instead of assigning 1, 2, and 8, you could have assigned 100, 200, and 800. It is the ratios that matter, not the actual numbers. How Planning Poker is played Now, let’s see how Planning Poker is played. Imagine you are in your Sprint Planning. 1- Each Developer has a deck of cards. 2- The PBI is discussed briefly by the Scrum Team. They try to understand the PBI through conversation. The Product Owner has a crucial role here as he is in direct contact with the market and stakeholders, knowing what their expectations are. Image 3- Each Developer individually selects a card that is his or her estimate. 4- Cards are turned over at the same time. So, all members can see them simultaneously. 5- The Scrum Team discusses differences specifically outliers. I mean those Developers who gave it the highest and lowest numbers. We ask them how they perceived the PBI. With a new round of conversation, all members get a better understanding of the work. 6- Re-estimate until estimates converge to one value. 7- You are there. You have estimated your PBI with the collective intelligence of the team. There are a few tips for playing Planning Poker: Tip 1: To play Planning Poker you need a baseline PBI because the item being estimated should be compared to one or more previously estimated items. Mr. Mike Cohn elaborated on this precisely. An advantage to relative estimating is that it becomes easier to do as a team estimates more items. Estimating a new item becomes a matter of looking at the previously estimated items and finding something requiring a similar amount of work. This is easier to do when the team has already estimated 100 items than when they’ve only estimated 10. But how about a team that just wants to start using Planning Poker in their process? The very basic solution is to identify a very simple PBI in your project that doesn’t need too much effort as the baseline and call it 1 Story Point then compare other PBIs with it. If you want a better solution, team members should identify two values that will establish their baseline. They do this without playing Planning Poker. They do it just through discussion. After the baseline is established, team members can use Planning Poker to estimate additional items. Ideally, the team is able to identify both a two-point PBI and a five-point PBI. Many other items can then be more reliably compared against the two and the five. If finding a two and a five proves difficult, look instead for a three and an eight. However, it is better to avoid starting with a one-point PBI. Because comparing all subsequent PBIs to a one-point PBI is difficult. Saying one product backlog item will take two or three times more effort than another seems intuitively easier and more accurate than saying something will take 10 times more effort. If a team has established a baseline with two- and five-point PBIs, team members can validate a three-point estimate by thinking about whether it will take more effort than the two and less effort than the five. items.summary: Image You know this meeting. The data is right there on the screen. Then the most senior person in the room says what they think, and the decision quietly bends to match, evidence or no evidence. Or it's the other version: someone frames the question in the first thirty seconds, a couple of people nod, and the room "agrees," while three people who saw it differently decide this isn't the moment to say so. Either way, the decision got made before the truth was even in the room. Not because anyone was careless. Because most meetings converge on the loudest or most senior voice long before the real information has a chance to land. Someone wrote down that the database choice had quietly stopped being the team's. The policy still said it was theirs. A business architect was making the call, and it was not their call to make. Nobody was going to say that out loud. At a niche insurer, two minutes of writing before anyone spoke started the argument that ended with the team choosing the database themselves, on the merits. There are two small repairs for this, and they target two different reasons it happens. Neither is a culture program. Both fit inside a meeting you're already having. Two ways the room decides too early The first reason is that the evidence is in the room and nobody has actually read it. The dashboard is open in a tab. The report went round on Friday. What gets discussed is everyone's impression of it, and the most confident impression wins. This is a failure of Honest Inspection, the team looking at the real state of the work and naming it truthfully. And the comfortable version has a documented lean: status reporting drifts optimistic, because marking something red triggers escalation while leaving it green costs nothing today. That's where a room drifts unless something anchors it to what can be shown. PMI's 2024 Project Success research puts a price on the drift: 81% of projects with risk monitoring in the measurement system reach a materially higher success score than projects without it. That is evidence that keeping an honest picture in front of the decision changes outcomes. It says nothing about whether a silent read is the way to get one. The second reason is that hierarchy suppresses independent voice. People have the dissenting thought and keep it, because saying it in front of senior people feels more costly than staying quiet. This is a failure of Trust and Candor. And it's the majority behavior, not the exception: in a 2025 Visier survey, about 46% of employees admitted they withhold honest feedback at work. That is people owning up to it in a survey, so treat it as the floor rather than the number. The real position exists. It just waits for the hallway. Repair one: read the evidence together, in silence Aim this at the room where the evidence is present and nobody has read it. Before anyone says what they think, the team reads it together, in silence. The test results, the customer signals, the outcome numbers, whatever the decision actually rests on. Nobody speaks until everyone has looked up. Your own view goes last, after theirs. Why it could help: the number already exists, it just has no route into the discussion until reading it is the first thing that happens in the room. Reading evidence as a group is a habit almost nobody has built, so it sits open in a tab while the conversation runs on what people remember of it. A possible sign it's working: people quote the thing they've just read rather than their memory of it, and the tab stops being opened and abandoned. The watch-out is specific, and it's the version most teams land on by accident: this turns into one person presenting the evidence to everyone else, and now the room is processing a speaker again. Reading together means each person reading it themselves. Not one person reading it aloud. Repair two: write before you talk Aim this at the room that goes quiet and calls it agreement. On anything contested, everyone writes their own view privately for two minutes before the discussion opens, and then the writing gets shared. You write yours at the same time and put it in the same batch, so nobody has to go first. Why it could help: speaking up in front of the person who decides your next raise carries a risk, and staying quiet carries none. The people with the least standing in the room work that out early, which is why inviting them to speak up leaves the risk exactly where it was. Writing first puts every view on the table before rank has filtered any of them. A possible sign it's working: positions appear that would not have survived being said second, and at least once a quiet person's note changes a decision that looked settled. The watch-out: writing is the first thing dropped when time is short, which is exactly when the pressure to converge is strongest, and if it only ever runs on the easy topics then the hard ones are still being decided the old way. items.title: The Organisation Owns the Minimum Definition of Done
items.summary: Originally published at Engineering Leadership on 21 October 2026 as The Organisation Owns the Minimum Definition of Done . The minimum Definition of Done exists to protect the business and its customers, so it belongs to the people accountable for them. Engineering informs it, and engineering should not have to set it: when it does, the business has given up a decision that is its own. Name the person who would answer to the board or the regulator if work shipped below it harmed a customer. If you cannot, nobody owns it yet. In the organisations I work with, the Definition of Done is usually left to engineering. It ends up describing what engineering can control (tests written, code reviewed, a pipeline passed) rather than what the business is exposed to. A leader reading it cannot tell whether the work protects customer data, meets accessibility duties, or keeps the company on the right side of its regulators. I have argued before that the Definition of Done should come from the business and be objective . Whoever owns the Definition of Done decides what happens when a deadline arrives When engineering owns the Definition of Done, I see three faults again and again. Scope gets in, as “meets acceptance criteria”. Numbers stand in for quality, as “80% code coverage”. Handoffs replace states, as “code reviewed” and “QA signed off”. Each of these is something engineering can tick without anyone accountable for the business looking at it. The more serious fault is what happens under pressure. A deadline arrives, the work is not ready, and somebody has to decide whether to ship. If the bar belongs to engineering, the pressure flows to engineering, and engineering is rarely in a position to refuse the people who set its deadlines. In my experience, the bar gets waived quietly once, and after that waivers become routine. My view is that whoever owns the bar decides what happens when it gets in the way. When the people accountable for the business own it, lowering it means one of them putting a name to that decision. That moves the decision to the people who carry the consequence. Many readers will hold a different model: engineering and the business own it jointly, with business sign-off. I think shared ownership leaves the bar negotiable between two owners at exactly the moment of pressure, and each can assume the other is holding it. One accountable owner, with engineering advising, does not have that gap. Engineers know how to achieve quality and how to show it. Knowing how is not the same as being accountable for the exposure. Leaders set the minimum; engineering advises on it and meets it. The Definition of Done is the minimum that protects the business and its customers What does the Definition of Done protect? In the organisations I work with, the answer usually includes security, privacy, accessibility, and legal and regulatory duties. The list is not complete. Each item is something the business answers for when it goes wrong, and each one is a duty to customers as much as to the company. It is a minimum, not a maximum. Products and teams go above it all the time, and they should. It is also never the whole of quality: a product can meet the Definition of Done and still be clumsy, slow, or unloved. For an organisation whose work is not yet live in production when it is called Done, I suggest something like this: Integrated into the main build, releasable, meeting our quality and security standards, and instrumented with telemetry that will support or weaken the hypothesis the work started from. Every phrase in that statement describes a condition of the work, with evidence attached to the work, that protects something the business cares about. None of it says how the team got there. Shipping work that is not Done harms the business and its customers Shipping work that has not reached the Definition of Done is a false value proposition: it looks like delivery, and I hold that it harms rather than helps. Low-quality work costs time, defects and money, and the studies below put figures on it. Tornhill and Borg found that low-quality code “contains 15 times more defects”, that issues took about 124% longer to resolve, and that maximum cycle times were about 9 times longer, though the authors work for CodeScene and used that vendor’s own measure of code quality [1]. Besker, Martini and Bosch reported that developers “waste, on average, 23% of their time due to TD” (technical debt), a figure the developers in the study reported themselves [2]. CISQ estimated the cost of poor software quality in the US at “at least $2.41 trillion”, with technical debt at about $1.52 trillion, a macro estimate that is not peer-reviewed [3]. DORA’s guidance states that “speed and stability are not tradeoffs”, which undercuts the idea that shipping below the minimum buys speed, though the finding comes from survey data and is correlational rather than causal [4]. One widely repeated claim does not survive scrutiny. Menzies and…

items.title: Ethical Aspects of Using AI in Products and Organizations
items.summary: Image Artificial intelligence is increasingly helping us make decisions, analyze data, create content, design solutions, write code, and automate work. With the rapid development of generative AI, these capabilities are expanding at an impressive pace. In organizations, we therefore ask: What can we do with AI? How can we use it faster? Where can it bring the greatest efficiency gains? What value can it create for customers and for the business? What I observe, however, is that we ask less often: Should we do it? And this is where the conversation about ethics begins. My academic background also includes philosophy. I have spent most of my professional career in the world of technology, agility, and product management. Perhaps this is why ethics has never felt like an abstract branch of philosophy to me. I am primarily interested in it as a way of looking at decisions: what values lie behind them, who they affect, what consequences they may have, and whether we are prepared to take responsibility for those consequences. Together with Patricia Kong, I explored this topic in the whitepaper Ethics in Product Management [1], published by Scrum.org. Our starting point was a simple observation: ethics does not suddenly become relevant only when we build a product that uses artificial intelligence. Product decisions have always had an ethical dimension. Products influence people’s behavior, their choices, and their access to information or services. We decide what data we collect, what we optimize for, what behaviors we encourage, and who may benefit from or be harmed by the solutions we create. AI did not create the problem of ethics. What AI has changed is the speed and scale at which the consequences of our decisions can emerge. It also means that many of these questions remain just as important, if not more so. Ethics Does Not Start with AI When we start talking about the ethics of artificial intelligence, terms such as bias, fairness, explainability, privacy, accountability, or, more broadly, Responsible AI quickly come up. It is also worth asking a more fundamental question: what does ethics actually mean in the context of technology and products? In their day-to-day work, organizations look at decisions from several different perspectives. One of them is technological feasibility: can we build it? Another is whether we are solving a real problem and creating value for customers. Will customers want to use it? Does the investment make sense for the organization? Another perspective involves law, regulation, security, data protection, and compliance. In other words: are we allowed to do it? In my view, we also need the question raised earlier: should we do it? Organizations do not always ask this question and this is where we enter the field of ethics. Let us look at it from another angle. Not every feature we are capable of building should be built. Not everything that can generate profit should necessarily be implemented. And even compliance with the law does not automatically tell us whether a particular decision is ethically sound. The law sets boundaries. Ethics, however, helps us make decisions in the vast space that exists within and beyond those boundaries. There are different ethical theories and frameworks, which means that the same decision can look very different depending on the perspective we adopt. We discuss these approaches in more detail, with examples, in Ethics in Product Management . Personalization or Manipulation? Imagine a product that, with the help of AI, can predict with a high degree of accuracy which message is most likely to persuade a particular user to make a purchase. From a technological perspective, this may be entirely feasible. From a business perspective, it may look like a success. Let us assume that conversion increases and revenue grows with it. The way the system operates may also be fully compliant with applicable regulations. And yet one question remains: at what point does personalization become manipulation? If we know that a user is in a particular emotional state, should we use that knowledge to make a sale more likely? If an algorithm discovers that creating anxiety increases engagement, should we optimize the product in that direction? And if a recommendation system can keep a user in an app 20% longer, is that necessarily a good outcome? Who Are We Creating Value For? This leads to one more question I would add to the earlier ones: For whom? A product may create value for the company while reducing value for the user. A solution may be valuable for some customers while excluding a particular group. An AI-based recruitment system may reduce the time needed to review hundreds of applications from several days to just a few minutes. But do we know on what basis it rejects candidates? Are certain groups being systematically assessed less favorably? And does a rejected candidate have any way to challenge the decision? The question “is this ethical?” rarely has a…

items.title: Customer Representative: The Difference Between a Hobby Product and Something Others Might Use?
items.summary: Image One of the things I’m trying to do as I develop Paper Drum is put into practice all the stuff that I’ve been doing over the last couple of decades in enterprise product delivery. Probably the thing that brings it all together in my mind is a training course that I’ve been delivering for some time called the Professional Scrum Product Owner - Advanced class. This class doesn’t talk about theory at all. It assumes you know all that. Instead, it delves into the six stances of effective Product Ownership. I was delivering this class over the last couple of days, and I realised that when it comes to the customer representative and understanding customers, I’ve been breaking several of my own rules. Now, I’ve been quite deliberately following the advice that I’ve been giving. One of the key bits of advice is that you’ve got to get out of your own head. You’ve got to talk to real users and understand customers. And so, at a very early stage in the development of Paper Drum, I scheduled half a dozen calls with people I know: people I’ve worked with in the past, even family. People who are supportive of me, and therefore I can take their praise with a pinch of salt and try to tease out criticism. You’ve got to get out of your own head. Now, some of these interviews did prompt some useful information. For example, one user opened the product up - in my head, this was something that you would open up, you would play around with, you would improvise some melodies or some music or some drum rhythms. You would explore, you would be curious. But for somebody that had never seen my product before, they saw a piano keyboard as the first screen. Instinctively, they tried to play a tune that they knew, a simple melody, and they couldn’t, because it wasn’t set up that way. That wasn’t a good experience, and then they didn’t really know what to do. So based on that, I understood that it would be better to have some sort of introductory learning segments: somebody teaching you a rhythm, and then easing you into making up your own things. Another useful thing that came out of these interviews was a question I’d scripted, which did work quite well: “would you be prepared to use this for a week and give me some feedback at the end?” And somebody said, “Well, actually, you know, I’m supportive of what you’re doing, but actually, no, I wouldn’t. And the reason is that as it is right now, I can’t really see the point of it. There’s nothing to say why it would be worth it, why I would come back time after time.” As it is right now, I can’t really see the point of it. So that gave me really useful insights into developing something that would answer that question. What would I do? Why would I come back to this? That prompted me to build a learning pathway that would lead into the ability to develop your own rhythms, and then potentially share them with others, and then come back to it. But as I was teaching the PSPO-A class just over the last couple of days, and reiterating the advice about how to talk to customers, how to talk to users, I realised I was doing several things that I was telling the class not to do. I realised I was doing several things that I was telling the class not to do. Firstly, I was solving problems there in the call. At one point in the discussion, somebody said that they couldn’t see what they were supposed to be doing. Rather than just note that and thank them for the feedback, I proceeded to talk them through it and demonstrate. Now, this is a good thing to do, and I think any product needs effective support. You need a way for people to figure out what to do. But the trouble is that if you do that in a conversation where you’re trying to learn about what’s working in the product and what’s not working, that information then doesn’t come through. The focus of the conversation is “let me show you this” or “let me explain that”. That doesn’t leave space for “here’s what I think, this is my experience”. And that’s the stuff that you want. That’s the stuff I was looking for. The other mistake I made is that I was essentially pitching the product. I was explaining my idea of how music in the past was participatory. People used to join in, whereas now it’s more productised. It’s something you buy, it’s something that you listen to. items.title: Making Product Decisions Before the Results Are In
items.summary: Some product outcomes take weeks to become visible, yet stakeholders may expect decisions much sooner. For a Product Owner, the challenge is understanding what the available evidence tells us and how to make decisions when the intended results are still uncertain. Image When the evidence is not yet available During my work on investment management software, I was involved with systems that helped financial institutions manage investments and maintain accurate records. One situation that illustrates this challenge concerned the monthly process of checking investment records against information received from banks. We were developing a feature designed to detect differences earlier, reducing the manual corrections employees needed to make during these checks. After releasing it to a limited group of users, a stakeholder asked at the following Sprint Review whether we were ready to make it available to more customers. The initial numbers looked promising. People were using the feature, and the dashboard showed fewer manual corrections. However, most customers had not yet completed their monthly checks, meaning that additional problems could still be discovered. We knew people were using the functionality, but we could not yet establish whether it was reducing the work we intended to address. Understand what the numbers actually show Our dashboard showed the percentage of investment portfolios requiring manual corrections. A portfolio is simply a collection of investments managed together. The problem was that our calculation included portfolios whose monthly checks were still in progress. Those awaiting final verification appeared to require no corrections, even though discrepancies might be discovered later. Consequently, the results could look better simply because much of the work remained unfinished. After discussing the process with operations, we agreed to evaluate only portfolios that had completed their monthly checks, comparing their results with previous periods using the same criteria. However, the Developers identified another issue: some corrections were performed outside the application and never appeared in the dashboard. Even after the monthly checks were complete, our numbers could still underestimate the actual manual work involved. We were facing two different problems. Some results needed more time to emerge, while others were missing from our records. Waiting would address the first issue, but the second required improving the information we collected. Until both were addressed, the apparent reduction in corrections was not sufficient evidence that the feature had achieved its intended outcome. Decide whether to expand the release The stakeholder still needed an answer, and delaying the release also had consequences. I proposed keeping the functionality limited to the existing group until the next monthly checks were completed and we had addressed the gaps in our data. Other customers would have to wait longer for a potentially useful improvement, but expanding immediately would mean accepting uncertainty about its impact. That did not mean waiting regardless of what happened. If we discovered that the feature was failing to detect important errors, we would need to respond immediately rather than wait for another monthly cycle. Together with stakeholders, we agreed on what to inspect at the next Sprint Review, including the number of completed checks and whether we could account for corrections performed outside the application. Once we had reliable results, we could compare the manual corrections required before and after introducing the feature. Even then, differences in portfolio complexity or changes in working procedures could influence the numbers, so an apparent improvement would not automatically mean the feature was responsible. By keeping the release limited, we avoided extending the feature based on results we could not yet trust. We also identified gaps in how manual corrections were recorded, which gave the Developers and operations something concrete to address. Stakeholders understood why we needed more evidence and what we would examine before reconsidering the release. Whether the feature actually reduced manual work was still an open question, but we now had a clearer way to evaluate it. Make uncertainty visible at the Sprint Review The Scrum Guide describes the Sprint Review as an opportunity for the Scrum Team and stakeholders to inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations. A usable Increment can also be delivered before the Sprint Review, since the event is not a release gate. In our situation, the Sprint Review allowed us to inspect the released Increment and discuss what we had learned, including the limitations of the available data. As Product Owner, I remained accountable for maximizing product value and effective Product Backlog management, while the discussion with stakeholders helped inform our next decisions. items.title: Scrum and AI - Outcomes and Boundaries
items.summary: Outcomes, Not Automation Boundaries Before Acceleration Reflections on Agile, Scrum and Human Accountability in the Age of AI Overview Artificial intelligence is transforming how organisations develop products, make decisions and deliver services. Tasks that previously required weeks may increasingly be completed in hours or minutes. Yet faster execution does not necessarily produce better business outcomes. As AI reduces the cost of producing solutions, the ability to identify valuable problems, test assumptions and respond to evidence becomes increasingly important. To achieve true competitive advantage from adopting AI, organisations will need to develop the capability of learning and adapting at speed. This will require clear accountability boundaries and constraints, as well as holding people accountable to honouring these constraints. 1. Faster Delivery Is Not Greater Value AI can help us deliver so much more quickly. It can speed up all aspects of product development; however, increased output doesn’t mean improved outcomes. The rapid delivery can also create more waste. Poor products, difficulties in maintenance, huge volumes of text to analyse, and hallucinations resulting in flawed assumptions. I have witnessed the scenario where people use AI to generate a long winded email, only to have the recipient use AI to summarise it! Organisations must distinguish between producing more (output focus) and achieving better outcomes. The risk of generating a lot of low-value output is real. Agile principles become increasingly relevant because they emphasise customer value, feedback, collaboration and adaptation. The fundamental question is not how quickly AI can deliver, but whether what it delivers creates measurable value. The key metric for adopting AI (or any practice, for that matter) should be real business outcomes. 2. Empiricism as a Competitive Advantage Scrum provides a practical framework for managing complexity through transparency, inspection and adaptation. The Scrum Events create regular opportunities to evaluate progress, challenge assumptions and adjust direction. As AI accelerates execution, these learning opportunities become increasingly important. The challenge is for leaders and organisations to apply a “Thinking in Bets” approach actively. The speed that we can test a hypothesis should be changing how we work on at every level of the organisation. At the highest Portfolio level, each Product should be using a build – deliver – review – learn approach. This pattern should be repeated from the very top of an organisation to the delivery team level. Objective, meaningful data based evidence should be used to guide the next decision. Every capital investment should be evaluated against the Return on Investment (ROI) proposition. I encourage using Evidence Based Management metrics to guide this, as I have seen this work well. 3. Empowerment Requires Organisational Change Organisations that actively embraced delegated authority are better placed to reap the benefits of using AI within their organisation. They have already streamlined the workflow to deliver to the customer. Alternative organisational approaches, including Haier's RenDanHeYi model (summarised in the https://www.zer0.guide/), demonstrate possibilities for greater entrepreneurial autonomy. This can be a seismic shift in the way that leaders work with their teams. The move towards holding the teams accountable within clear boundaries encourages teams at all levels to focus on delivery. Leaders should establish clear purpose, constraints and decision-making authority, enabling teams to experiment and respond directly to customer needs. However, autonomy requires coordination. Shared standards, transparent priorities and enterprise-wide objectives remain essential. The goal is not to eliminate leadership, but to change how leadership enables value creation. 4. Human Accountability in an Autonomous World AI agents will increasingly conduct experiments, analyse opportunities and make operational decisions. Human oversight must remain meaningful rather than ceremonial. Within Scrum, the Product Owner remains accountable for maximising product value, while AI may support analysis, experimentation, and decision-making. Autonomy should reflect risk. Routine, reversible decisions can be delegated more extensively, while consequential strategic, financial and ethical decisions require appropriate human authority. Human control means retaining the ability to understand, challenge, redirect and stop autonomous activity. This means organisations must develop people to sustain business continuity, so younger or newer people develop the critical thinking and requisite skills to direct agentic systems. 5. items.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel: at extreme speeds, the light propelling futuristic solar sails could actually begin slowing them down. Once a spacecraft reaches 75% of the speed of light, some scattered light starts producing drag, potentially complicating humanity’s plans to reach distant stars.

items.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
items.summary: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

items.title: A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that a common blood pressure drug can activate calorie-burning brown fat in mice, potentially opening a new path toward improving metabolic health. An analysis of more than 100,000 patients also revealed surprising links between brown fat and lower rates of heart disease, diabetes, anxiety, and depression.

items.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
items.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

items.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
items.summary: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.
